title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
content:
OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.
The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

report.summary: OpenAI has raised $11 billion so far in a new round at a $1.25 trillion valuation, with the round expected to reach about $20 billion.
report.background: The raise lands in an AI capital boom defined by massive compute spending, data-center buildouts, and a race to secure talent and chips. OpenAI and rivals have signed multibillion-dollar infrastructure deals and pursued ever-larger private rounds to fund training and inference. But investor appetite is being tested: OpenAI had reportedly sought $30 billion, and the current round may close around $20 billion. Public markets are also sending mixed signals—Anthropic IPO buyers are eyeing a much lower valuation than earlier expectations. Meanwhile, AI has become politically contentious. The U.S. midterms produced a Democratic landslide, and local opposition to data centers has grown over energy use, water, and land. That combination—huge capital needs, uncertain public-market demand, and rising regulatory risk—frames OpenAI’s fundraising and its delayed IPO plans.
key_points: OpenAI has secured $11 billion so far in a funding round that values it at $1.25 trillion. The round is still open and could total about $20 billion, people familiar told Bloomberg. That is below the roughly $30 billion OpenAI reportedly sought in September, suggesting investors remain enthusiastic but are pushing back on the most aggressive targets.

The capital gives OpenAI room to keep spending on chips, data centers, model training, and talent without immediately depending on public markets. OpenAI had signaled an IPO this year but delayed it; expectations now point to a listing next year. Private money acts as a bridge while the company scales and waits for clearer market conditions.

Competitor Anthropic is seeing cooler demand ahead of its IPO. Potential buyers reportedly value it as low as $1.1 trillion, down from about $2 trillion expected a month earlier. The gap shows public investors may be more valuation-sensitive than private backers, a warning sign for the entire AI sector.

The fundraising comes amid political turbulence. A Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms and negative voter sentiment around data centers have rattled AI markets. Candidates and communities have raised concerns about energy use, water consumption, and local costs. Investors may price in slower permitting and tougher regulation for AI infrastructure.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the round confirms that private capital can still fund mega-scale AI even as public-market investors grow pickier. That favors incumbents with compute and distribution, and raises pressure on smaller labs to find niches or partners. For developers, OpenAI’s funding supports continued API and model investment, but monetization pressure could bring pricing changes, tighter usage policies, or more enterprise-focused releases. Rivals will try to compete on price and openness. For regular users, the practical effect is likely more capable assistants and tools, but also more ads, subscriptions, or usage limits as companies chase returns. Political backlash against data centers could slow deployments and affect local energy costs, making regulatory risk a consumer issue too.
report.tools: To track the deal, watch Bloomberg, TechCrunch, Crunchbase, and PitchBook; for IPO signals, monitor SEC EDGAR filings. To try the technology, use OpenAI’s API/Playground, Anthropic’s Claude, and open-source stacks such as Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, Ollama, Llama, and Mistral. For infrastructure context, follow MLPerf benchmarks and U.S. EIA energy data.
